ch03.title: The Carpenter's Child
ch03.b002: The months in Bethlehem had been full of uncertainty and fear, and Mary did not wean the baby until the family had arrived safely in Alexandria, where at last they could settle down to a normal life. They lived with kinsfolk, and Joseph soon found work. For several months he was employed as a carpenter, and then he was raised to foreman of a large group of workmen on one of the public buildings then under construction. The experience gave him the idea of becoming a contractor and builder once they returned to Nazareth.
ch03.b003: All through these years of her child’s helpless infancy, Mary kept one long and constant vigil, lest anything befall him that might endanger his welfare or interfere with his future mission. No mother was ever more devoted to her child. There were other children about his age in the house and among the neighbors. At first Mary wanted to keep Jesus close by her side; she feared something might happen to him if he played in the garden with the others. But Joseph, with the help of his kinsfolk, convinced her that such sheltering would deprive the boy of learning how to get along with children of his own age. Mary gave her assent to letting the child of promise grow up just like any other child. Still, she made it her business always to be on watch while the little ones played about the house and garden.
ch03.b004: Jesus enjoyed good health in Alexandria and grew normally. Apart from a few friends and relatives, no one was told that he was a “child of promise.” But shortly before the family left Egypt, a few friends in Memphis, descendants of the distant Ikhnaton, and a small group of Alexandrian believers gathered at the palatial home of Joseph’s relative and benefactor to wish the Nazareth family well. On that occasion they presented Jesus with a complete copy of the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures. The gift was not placed in Joseph’s hands, though, until he and Mary had finally declined the invitation of these friends to remain in Egypt. The believers insisted that the child of destiny could exert a far greater influence on the world as a resident of Alexandria than of any place in Palestine, and their persuasions delayed the family’s departure for some time after the news of Herod’s death had come.
ch03.b006: At length Joseph and Mary took leave of Alexandria on a boat belonging to their friend Ezraeon, bound for Joppa, and arrived there late in August of 4 B.C. They went straight to Bethlehem and spent the whole of September in counsel with friends and relatives over whether to remain there or return to Nazareth.
ch03.b007: Mary had never fully given up the idea that Jesus ought to grow up in Bethlehem, the City of David. To her it seemed the most fitting place in which to rear a new candidate for David’s throne. Joseph did not really believe that their son was to be a kingly deliverer of Israel. Besides, he knew that he himself was not truly a descendant of David, but was only reckoned so because one of his ancestors had been adopted into the Davidic line. And he was afraid. Herod was dead, but his son Archelaus now ruled in Judea, and Joseph surmised that Archelaus would be more likely than Herod Antipas in Galilee to pursue his father’s menacing policies. He preferred to take his chances with Antipas. He was outspoken, too, in his belief that Galilee was the better place to rear and educate the child. It took him three weeks to overcome Mary’s objections.
ch03.b008: By the first of October Joseph had convinced Mary and all their friends that it was best to return to Nazareth. Early in October, 4 B.C., they set out early one Sunday morning, going by way of Lydda and Scythopolis. Mary and the child rode the beast of burden they had lately acquired, and Joseph walked with five kinsmen who refused to let the little family make the journey alone.
ch03.b010: On the fourth day the party reached Nazareth in safety. They arrived unannounced at their own house, which one of Joseph’s married brothers had been living in for more than three years. He was indeed surprised to see them; they had gone about their affairs so quietly that neither Joseph’s family nor Mary’s knew they had even left Alexandria. The next day the brother moved his family out, and for the first time since Jesus’ birth, Mary settled down with her little family in a home of their own. In less than a week Joseph had found work as a carpenter, and they were supremely happy.
ch03.b011: Jesus was about three years and two months old. He was full of childish glee at having premises of his own to run about in, though he greatly missed his playmates in Alexandria. On the road, Joseph had persuaded Mary that it would be unwise to tell their Galilean friends and relatives that Jesus was a child of promise, and they agreed to say nothing of these matters to anyone. Both kept the promise faithfully.
ch03.b012: His fourth year was a time of normal physical growth and unusual mental activity. He formed a close attachment to a neighbor boy of about his own age named Jacob, and the two grew up great friends and loyal companions. In the early morning hours of April 2, 3 B.C., the second child, James, was born. Jesus was thrilled to have a baby brother and would stand around by the hour just watching him.
ch03.b013: That midsummer Joseph built a small workshop close to the village spring, near the lot where the caravans stopped to rest. From then on he did very little carpentry by the day. He sent out two of his brothers and several other mechanics to work, while he stayed at the shop making yokes and plows and doing other woodwork, and some work in leather, rope, and canvas. As Jesus grew, when he was not at school, he divided his time between helping his mother at home and watching his father at the shop, listening all the while to the talk of caravan drivers and travelers from the four corners of the earth.
ch03.b014: In July, a month before Jesus turned four, a malignant intestinal sickness spread over Nazareth from contact with the caravan travelers. Mary was so alarmed that she bundled up both children and fled to her brother’s farm, several miles south of Nazareth on the Megiddo road near Sarid. They stayed more than two months, and Jesus greatly enjoyed his first experience of life on a farm.
ch03.b016: A little more than a year after the return to Nazareth, the boy reached the age of his first personal and wholehearted moral decision. On February 11, 2 B.C., there came to abide with him a Thought Adjuster, a divine gift of the Paradise Father, which had aforetime served with Machiventa Melchizedek, and so had experience in functioning with the incarnation of a supermortal being living in the likeness of mortal flesh. Jesus was no more aware of the coming of this divine Monitor than are the millions upon millions of other children who, before and since that day, have received Thought Adjusters to indwell their minds and work for the spiritualization of those minds and the eternal survival of their immortal souls.
ch03.b017: On that day in February the direct and personal supervision of the Universe Rulers over the integrity of Michael’s childlike incarnation came to an end. From then on, the guardianship of Jesus rested with the indwelling Adjuster and the associated seraphic guardians, supplemented from time to time by midway creatures assigned to particular duties.
ch03.b018: That summer, on the night of July 11, a little more than a month before his fifth birthday, his sister Miriam was born, and Jesus was made very happy. The most valuable part of his early education came from his parents in answer to his thoughtful and searching questions, and Joseph never failed to take pains and time over them. From the age of five until he was ten, Jesus was one continuous question mark. His parents could not always answer, but they never failed to talk the matter through with him and help him toward a satisfying answer of his own. Jesus was of great help to his mother in caring for his little brother and baby sister.
ch03.b019: It was the custom of the Galilean Jews for the mother to be responsible for a child’s training until the fifth birthday, after which a boy’s education became the father’s responsibility. And so on August 21, 2 B.C., Mary formally turned Jesus over to Joseph for further instruction. She still taught him at home, though. She showed him how to know and care for the vines and flowers along the garden walls, and on the roof of the house, the summer bedroom, she set out shallow boxes of sand in which he drew maps and practiced writing Aramaic, Greek, and later Hebrew. In time he learned to read, write, and speak all three languages fluently. Had you been there, you would have seen only a normal, healthy, carefree, but exceedingly inquisitive child of that time and place.
ch03.b020: What Even Father Did Not Know
ch03.b021: In his sixth year Joseph began to teach him Greek. Mary spoke little Greek, but Joseph spoke it fluently, and their textbook was the copy of the Hebrew scriptures that had been given them on leaving Egypt. There were only two complete copies of the Scriptures in Greek in all Nazareth, and owning one of them made the carpenter’s house a much-sought place, so that Jesus, as he grew, met an almost endless procession of earnest students and sincere seekers after truth. On his sixth birthday he was told that the book had been a gift to him from friends in Alexandria, and before the year was out he had taken charge of the priceless manuscript. In a very short time he could read it readily.
ch03.b022: The first great shock of his young life came when he was not quite six. It had seemed to him that his father, or at least his father and mother together, knew everything. So it was a great surprise when he asked Joseph the cause of a mild earthquake that had just shaken the town and heard him say, “⟦Q 123:3.2⟧My son, I really do not know.⟦/Q⟧” Thus began a long and disconcerting disillusionment, in which Jesus found out that his earthly parents were not all-wise and all-knowing. Even as a child Jesus was not satisfied when physical events were thoughtlessly put down to God or the devil. He long accepted good and evil spirits as a possible explanation of mental and spiritual things, but he very early began to doubt that such unseen influences caused the happenings of the natural world.
ch03.b023: In the early summer of 1 B.C., before Jesus was six, Zacharias and Elizabeth came to visit with their son John. It was the first meeting the two boys could remember. The visitors could stay only a few days, and while the parents talked over many things, including the future of their sons, the boys played with blocks in the sand on the housetop. After meeting John, Jesus began to take an unusual interest in the history of Israel and asked in great detail about the Sabbath rites, the synagogue sermons, and the feasts of the year, and his father explained them all, from the midwinter festival of lights to the joyful feast of tabernacles, when the whole people camped out in leafy booths.
ch03.b024: That year his parents had trouble with him over his prayers. He insisted on talking to his heavenly Father much as he talked to Joseph, his earthly father. This departure from more solemn forms was a bit disconcerting, especially to his mother, but there was no persuading him to change. He would say his prayers just as he had been taught, and then he insisted on having “⟦Q 123:3.6⟧just a little talk with my Father in heaven.⟦/Q⟧”
ch03.b025: In June of that year Joseph turned the shop over to his brothers and formally entered upon his work as a builder. Before the year was out the family income had more than trebled, and never again, until after Joseph’s death, did the family feel the pinch of poverty. As James grew old enough to help at home, Jesus often went with his father to building jobs in Cana, Magdala, Nain, Sepphoris, Capernaum, and Endor, a keen observer storing up knowledge about men and the way they lived. In his spare time he studied the flowers and plants by day and the stars by night, and he had a troublesome habit of lying on his back gazing up into the starry heavens long after his bedtime.
ch03.b027: Early in January of A.D. 1 a great snowstorm swept over Galilee. Snow fell two feet deep, the heaviest snowfall Jesus saw in his lifetime and one of the deepest at Nazareth in a hundred years. That spring, on Wednesday morning, March 16, A.D. 1, the fourth child, Joseph, was born.
ch03.b028: Jewish children of that day had few organized games; they mostly played at the serious things they saw their elders doing, at weddings and funerals. Jesus, with a neighbor boy and later with James, loved to play in the far corner of the carpenter shop, where they had great fun with the shavings and blocks of wood. He had a capacity for humor and play that his day afforded little room for, yet up to the age of fourteen he was cheerful and lighthearted most of the time.
ch03.b029: That July an unexpected sandstorm blew in from the east. Such hot winds, carrying blasts of fine sand, usually came in the rainy season, in March and April, and a July storm was extraordinary. Jesus was playing on the housetop, his usual playroom in the dry season, and as he came down the back-yard stone stairs he was blinded by the sand and fell. It was the only real accident he had had up to that time. Afterward Joseph built a balustrade up both sides of the stairway.
ch03.b030: The accident could not have been prevented. It was not the fault of the midway guardians, one primary and one secondary midwayer, who watched over the boy, nor of the guardian seraphim. Material accidents, the commonplace happenings of physical life, are not arbitrarily interfered with by celestial personalities. But because it happened while Joseph was away in Endor, it made Mary so anxious that she unwisely kept Jesus close by her side for some months. It was only one of a number of such minor mishaps that befell this inquisitive and adventurous boy.
ch03.b031: Synagogue School and Sabbaths on the Hill
ch03.b032: In August of that year, at seven, Jesus entered the synagogue school. He already read, wrote, and spoke Aramaic and Greek, and now he set out eagerly to learn Hebrew. The pupils sat on the floor in a semicircle facing their teacher, the chazan, an officer of the synagogue. The chazan would say a sentence, and the pupils would repeat it after him in unison. They began with Leviticus and went on through the other books of the law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. Following the custom, each new pupil chose a “birthday text” to guide him through his studies. Jesus chose from the Prophet Isaiah: “⟦Q 123:5.11⟧The spirit of the Lord God is upon me, for the Lord has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the meek, to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and to set the spiritual prisoners free.⟦/Q⟧”
ch03.b033: Nazareth was a caravan way station, largely gentile in population, and known as a center of liberal interpretation of Jewish law; hence the saying in Jerusalem, “⟦Q 123:5.7⟧Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?⟦/Q⟧” Galilean practice was more liberal regarding the Sabbath, too, and Joseph would take him walking on Sabbath afternoons. Their favorite climb was the high hill near their home. To the northwest the long ridge of Mount Carmel ran down to the sea, and Jesus heard his father tell again the story of Elijah. To the north Mount Hermon raised its snowy peak. Far to the east lay the Jordan valley and the rocky hills of Moab; to the south and east the marble walls of the Decapolis cities shone in the sun; and toward sunset, to the west, they could make out sailing vessels on the distant Mediterranean. Below, caravans wound in and out of Nazareth from four directions, and southward stretched the broad plain of Esdraelon toward Mount Gilboa and Samaria.
ch03.b034: Before he was eight, all the mothers and young women of Nazareth knew him from their talks at the spring. He learned to milk the family cow, to make cheese, and to weave, and by ten he was an expert at the loom. He and Jacob became great friends of Nathan the potter, who worked near the spring, and many times, watching his deft fingers mold the clay, both boys resolved to be potters when they grew up.
ch03.b036: In A.D. 2 Jesus belonged to the more progressive third of his class and did so well that he was excused from school one week in every month. That week he spent with his fisherman uncle on the Sea of Galilee near Magdala or on the farm of his mother’s brother south of Nazareth, and his aunts and uncles competed lively for his company. He traded dairy products for lessons on the harp, at which he became, by eleven, a skillful player. At school he kept asking embarrassing questions, such as why Palestine had a dry season and a rainy season. On Friday evening, April 14, his brother Simon was born.
ch03.b037: In February of that year Nahor, a teacher in a Jerusalem academy of the rabbis, came to Nazareth at the instigation of Zacharias to observe Jesus. At first he was somewhat shocked by the boy’s frankness and unconventional manner in religious things, but he put that down to the remoteness of Galilee and advised Joseph and Mary to let him take Jesus to Jerusalem to be educated at the center of Jewish culture. Mary was half persuaded; she was convinced her son was to be the Messiah. Joseph hesitated. He believed Jesus would be a man of destiny, but what that destiny would be he was profoundly uncertain, and the more he thought about it, the more he doubted the wisdom of the plan.
ch03.b038: Because the parents disagreed, Nahor asked leave to lay the whole matter before Jesus himself. The boy listened attentively and talked with Joseph, with Mary, and with their neighbor Jacob the stone mason, whose son was his favorite playmate. Two days later he gave his answer. Since his parents and advisers differed, and since he did not feel competent to take the responsibility for such a decision, he had decided to “⟦Q 123:6.9⟧talk with my Father who is in heaven.⟦/Q⟧” He was not perfectly sure of the answer, but he rather felt he should remain at home “with my father and mother,” adding, “⟦Q 123:6.9⟧they who love me so much should be able to do more for me and guide me more safely than strangers who can only view my body and observe my mind but can hardly truly know me.⟦/Q⟧”
ch03.b039: They all marveled, and Nahor went his way, back to Jerusalem. It was many years before the question of Jesus’ leaving home came up again.
ch04.title: The Boy Who Asked Questions
ch04.b001: A.D. 3 · The Drawing on the Schoolroom Floor
ch04.b002: Had he stayed in Alexandria, Jesus might have had better schooling, but it would have been directed by Jews and along exclusively Jewish lines. In Nazareth he worked out his own life problems with a minimum of educational guidance, and every day he met men and women of all classes from every part of the civilized world. It was a training that prepared him to understand the gentiles, and it gave him a more balanced idea of the Eastern and Western views of Hebrew theology.
ch04.b003: In the late winter of his ninth year came the most serious trouble he had yet had at school. Jesus delighted in drawing landscapes and in modeling all kinds of objects in potter’s clay. Everything of that sort was strictly forbidden by Jewish law as idolatrous, but until then he had managed to disarm his parents’ objections. Then one of the more backward pupils discovered him drawing a charcoal picture of the teacher on the floor of the schoolroom. There it was, plain as day, and many of the elders had seen it before a committee went to call on Joseph and demand that something be done to suppress the lawlessness of his eldest son.
ch04.b004: Jesus sat for some time on a large stone just outside the back door, listening to the indictment of his artistic efforts. But when he heard them blaming his father for his misdeeds, he resented it, and in he marched to confront his accusers. The elders were thrown into confusion. Some were inclined to take the episode humorously; one or two seemed to think the boy sacrilegious if not blasphemous. Joseph was nonplused and Mary indignant, but Jesus insisted on being heard. He had his say and courageously defended his viewpoint, and then, with consummate self-control, he announced that he would abide by his father’s decision in this as in all other matters of controversy. The committee of elders departed in silence.
ch04.b005: Mary tried to persuade Joseph to let the boy model in clay at home, provided he did nothing of the kind at school. But Joseph felt bound to rule that the rabbinical interpretation of the second commandment must prevail. From that day Jesus drew or modeled the likeness of nothing as long as he lived in his father’s house. He was not convinced that he had done wrong, and giving up so favorite a pastime was one of the great trials of his young life.
ch04.b007: In the latter part of June he climbed with his father to the summit of Mount Tabor for the first time. It was a clear day and the view was superb. To the nine-year-old boy it seemed that he had gazed upon the entire world excepting India, Africa, and Rome.
ch04.b008: On Thursday night, September 13, his second sister, Martha, was born. Three weeks later Joseph, home for a while, began building an addition to the house, a combined workshop and bedroom. A small workbench was made for Jesus, and for the first time he had tools of his own. At odd times for many years he worked at that bench and became highly expert in the making of yokes. That winter and the next were the coldest in Nazareth for many decades, and for the first time Jesus saw ice. He had long pondered the steam escaping from the boiling pots, and now the fact that water could be a solid, a liquid, and a vapor set him thinking a great deal about the physical world and its constitution. And yet the personality embodied in this growing boy was all the while the actual creator and organizer of all these things throughout a far-flung universe.
ch04.b009: In May, on his uncle’s farm, he helped for the first time with the grain harvest. Before he was thirteen he had found out something about practically every kind of work that men and women did around Nazareth, except metal working. He went often with his father to Cana, Endor, and Nain, and he visited Sepphoris, a little over three miles to the northwest, then the capital of Galilee and one of the residences of Herod Antipas. He was an original thinker and a skillful teacher even in his youth, and by now his parents were beginning to learn from him as well as to teach him. Before he was ten he had become the leader of a group of seven boys who formed a society for promoting the acquirements of manhood, physical, intellectual, and religious, and among them he introduced many new games and better methods of physical recreation.
ch04.b011: It was the fifth of July, the first Sabbath of the month. Strolling through the countryside with his father, Jesus first gave expression to feelings and ideas that showed he was becoming self-conscious of the unusual nature of his life mission. Joseph listened attentively to the momentous words of his son, but he made few comments and volunteered no information. The next day Jesus had a similar but longer talk with his mother. Mary, too, listened, and neither did she volunteer any information. It was almost two years before he spoke to his parents again about this growing revelation within his own consciousness.
ch04.b012: In August he entered the advanced school of the synagogue. There he was constantly creating trouble by the questions he persisted in asking, and he kept all Nazareth in more or less of a hubbub. His parents were loath to forbid him, and his chief teacher was greatly intrigued by the boy’s curiosity, insight, and hunger for knowledge.
ch04.b013: His playmates saw nothing supernatural in him; in most ways he was altogether like themselves. Perhaps his most unusual trait was his unwillingness to fight for his rights. He was well developed for his age, and it seemed strange to his playfellows that he would not defend himself even against injustice or personal abuse. He did not suffer much for it, thanks to Jacob, the stone mason’s son, a year older than he, who was a great admirer of Jesus and made it his business to see that no one imposed upon him. Several times older and uncouth youths attacked Jesus, relying on his reputed docility, but they always suffered swift and certain retribution at the hands of his self-appointed champion. Jesus was the accepted leader of the Nazareth boys who stood for the higher ideals of their day, and he was loved, not only because he was fair, but because he possessed a rare and understanding sympathy.
ch04.b014: That year he began to show a marked preference for the company of older people. He delighted in talking over things cultural, social, economic, political, and religious with older minds, and his depth of reasoning so charmed them that they were always glad to visit with him. His parents kept trying to steer him toward companions of his own age. Late in the year he spent two months fishing with his uncle on the Sea of Galilee, very successfully; before he reached manhood he was an expert fisherman. On his first visit to the fishing industry he had nearly made up his mind to become a fisherman. Later his father’s trade drew him toward carpentry, and still later a combination of influences led him to his final choice: to become a religious teacher of a new order.
ch04.b016: About the middle of May in his eleventh year he went with his father on a business trip to Scythopolis, the chief Greek city of the Decapolis, the ancient Hebrew Beth-shean. On the way Joseph told the old history of King Saul and the Philistines. But Jesus was tremendously impressed by the clean and well-ordered appearance of this so-called heathen city. He marveled at the open-air theater and admired the beautiful marble temple dedicated to the “heathen” gods. Joseph, much perturbed, extolled the grandeur of the temple at Jerusalem. It happened that the annual games of the Decapolis cities were in progress at the amphitheater, and Jesus was so insistent that his father take him that Joseph hesitated to refuse. The boy was thrilled and entered heartily into the spirit of the contests.
ch04.b017: After the games, Jesus expressed his approval of them and suggested that it would be good for the young men of Nazareth to benefit from such wholesome outdoor activity. Joseph talked with him long and earnestly about the evil nature of such practices, but he could see that the boy was unconvinced. Then, that night in their room at the inn, Jesus so far forgot the trend of Jewish thought as to suggest that they go home and work for the building of an amphitheater at Nazareth. Joseph forgot his usual calm. He seized his son by the shoulder and angrily exclaimed, “⟦Q 124:3.8⟧My son, never again let me hear you give utterance to such an evil thought as long as you live.⟦/Q⟧”
ch04.b018: It was the only time Jesus ever saw his father angry with him. He was astonished and shocked beyond expression, and he only replied, “⟦Q 124:3.8⟧Very well, my father, it shall be so.⟦/Q⟧” Never again, as long as his father lived, did he allude to the games of the Greeks. Yet throughout his life he sought to bring the idea of wholesome recreation into his own plans and, as far as Jewish practice allowed, into the life of his twelve apostles.
ch04.b019: On Wednesday evening, June 24, A.D. 5, the seventh child, Jude, was born. The birth brought complications, and Mary was so very ill for several weeks that Joseph stayed at home. Jesus was kept busy with errands and with the many duties his mother’s illness brought. From that time, just before he was eleven, he was compelled to take up the responsibilities of the first-born son, a year or two before such burdens would normally have fallen on him, and never again could he return to the childlike attitude of his earlier years. The chazan spent one evening each week helping him master the Hebrew scriptures, though he could never understand why his promising pupil was so indifferent to the prospect of going to Jerusalem to study under the learned rabbis.
ch04.b020: A.D. 6 · The Parchment on the Doorpost
ch04.b021: In his twelfth year Jesus began regular work in the home carpenter shop and was allowed to manage his own earnings, a very unusual arrangement in a Jewish family. He also learned the wisdom of keeping such matters within the family. He was becoming aware of how much trouble he had caused in the village, and from then on he grew increasingly discreet about anything that might make him seem different from his fellows. That year brought many seasons of uncertainty, if not actual doubt, about the nature of his mission. His naturally developing human mind did not yet fully grasp the reality of his dual nature.
ch04.b022: He often heard his parents discussing him when they thought he was sound asleep, and he became keenly aware of how differently they viewed his mission. More and more he inclined to his father’s view, and Mary was destined to be hurt as she came to realize that her son was gradually rejecting her guidance about his life career. Increasingly Joseph and Mary sensed that something superhuman dwelt in their eldest son, but they never even faintly dreamed that he was in truth the creator of this local universe. They lived and died without ever learning it.
ch04.b023: During his last year at school he remonstrated with his father about the custom of touching the bit of parchment nailed upon the doorpost on going in or out of the house, then kissing the finger that had touched it, while saying, “⟦Q 124:4.7⟧The Lord shall preserve our going out and our coming in, from this time forth and even forevermore.⟦/Q⟧” His parents had taught him again and again not to make images, because they might be used for idolatrous purposes. Jesus had never fully grasped that prohibition, but he had a high sense of consistency, and he pointed out to his father the essentially idolatrous nature of this habitual obeisance to the doorpost parchment. Joseph removed the parchment.
ch04.b024: Through this year and the two that followed, Jesus suffered great mental distress in trying to adjust his own views to the established beliefs of his parents. Two great commands contended in his young mind. The one was: “⟦Q 124:4.9⟧Be loyal to the dictates of your highest convictions of truth and righteousness.⟦/Q⟧” The other was: “⟦Q 124:4.9⟧Honor your father and mother, for they have given you life and the nurture thereof.⟦/Q⟧” He never shirked the daily work of reconciling them, and in time he achieved an increasingly harmonious blending of personal conviction and family obligation, a concept of group solidarity based upon loyalty, fairness, tolerance, and love.
ch05.title: The Pilgrimage at Twelve
ch05.b001: March, A.D. 7 · Son of the Commandment
ch05.b002: In this year the boy of Nazareth passed from boyhood to the beginning of young manhood. His voice began to change, and other signs of mind and body showed that manhood was coming on. On Sunday night, January 9, his baby brother Amos was born. About the middle of February Jesus became humanly assured that he was destined to perform a mission on earth for the enlightenment of man and the revelation of God. To outward appearances he was an average Jewish lad of Nazareth, but momentous decisions and far-reaching plans were forming in his mind, and the intelligent life of all Nebadon looked on with fascination and amazement.
ch05.b003: On the first day of the week, March 20, A.D. 7, Jesus graduated from the school of the Nazareth synagogue. It was a great day for any ambitious Jewish family, the day the first-born son was pronounced a “son of the commandment,” the ransomed first-born of the Lord God of Israel, a “child of the Most High.” Joseph had come over from Sepphoris, where he was in charge of work on a new public building, to be present. Jesus’ teacher confidently believed his pupil was destined for some distinguished mission, and the elders, for all their trouble with his nonconformist ways, were proud of him and had already begun planning to send him to the renowned academies in Jerusalem.
ch05.b004: As he heard these plans discussed, Jesus grew more and more sure that he would never go to Jerusalem to study with the rabbis. But he little dreamed of the tragedy, so soon to come, that would end all such plans by placing upon him the support of a large family, presently to number five brothers and three sisters, as well as his mother and himself.
ch05.b006: Now that he had graduated, Jesus was qualified to go up with his parents to celebrate his first Passover. The feast fell that year on Saturday, April 9. Women seldom went to the Passover; they were not required to be present. But Jesus virtually refused to go unless his mother came too, and when Mary decided to go, many other Nazareth women joined the journey, so that this company had the largest proportion of women ever to go up to the Passover from Nazareth. Early on Monday morning, April 4, a company of one hundred and three set out, and from time to time along the way they chanted the one hundred and thirtieth Psalm.
ch05.b007: To avoid passing through Samaria they turned east at Jezreel and went around Mount Gilboa into the Jordan valley. They passed Shunem, where Jesus heard again of the most beautiful maiden of Israel and of the works of Elisha; at Jezreel his parents told of Ahab and Jezebel and Jehu; around Gilboa they spoke of Saul and David. On the right they could see the marble buildings of Scythopolis, but they kept away from the gentile city lest they be defiled for the Passover. Mary could not understand why neither Joseph nor Jesus would say a word about Scythopolis. They had never told her of their quarrel there the year before.
ch05.b008: Then the road went down into the tropical Jordan valley, and Jesus saw for the first time the crooked, ever-winding river with its glistening waters. The pilgrims laid aside their outer garments and walked south past luxuriant fields of grain and oleanders heavy with pink blossoms, while far to the north snow-capped Mount Hermon looked down in majesty on the valley. That first night they camped by a bubbling spring under the starlit heavens. The second day they passed the mouth of the Jabbok and recalled the days of Gideon, and they camped near the base of Mount Sartaba, crowned by the Alexandrian fortress. On the third evening they reached Jericho, and Joseph, Mary, and Jesus walked a mile and a half to the site of ancient Jericho, where Joshua, for whom Jesus was named, had performed his renowned exploits.
ch05.b010: On the fourth day the road was a continuous procession of pilgrims climbing toward Jerusalem. About halfway up, Jesus had his first view of the Mount of Olives, and when Joseph told him that the Holy City lay just beyond that ridge, the boy’s heart beat fast with joyous anticipation of soon beholding the city and house of his heavenly Father.
ch05.b011: On the eastern slopes of Olivet they rested at the edge of a little village called Bethany. The villagers poured out to minister to the pilgrims, and Joseph’s family happened to stop near the house of one Simon, who had three children about Jesus’ age: Mary, Martha, and Lazarus. They invited the Nazareth family in for refreshment, and a lifelong friendship sprang up between the two families.
ch05.b012: Then they pressed on and stood on the brink of Olivet, and Jesus saw for the first time in his memory the Holy City, its pretentious palaces, and the inspiring temple of his Father. At no time in his life did he ever experience such a purely human thrill as on that April afternoon. In after years, on this same spot, he would stand and weep over the city that was about to reject the last and greatest of her heavenly teachers.
ch05.b014: It was Thursday afternoon when they came into the city and passed the temple. Jesus had never seen such throngs, and he pondered how these Jews had gathered from the uttermost parts of the known world. They lodged with a well-to-do relative of Mary’s, and while Jerusalem was astir with preparations, Joseph took his son to see the academy where he was to begin his studies at fifteen. He was truly puzzled at how little interest the boy showed.
ch05.b015: With his parents Jesus passed through the temple precincts to join the new sons of the law who were to be consecrated. The first great shock of the day came when his mother left them for the women’s gallery. It had never occurred to him that she would not be with him at the consecration, and he was thoroughly indignant at such unjust discrimination, though apart from a few words of protest to his father, he said nothing. The rituals themselves seemed perfunctory to him, lacking the personal warmth of the synagogue at Nazareth.
ch05.b016: Everywhere in the temple courts he was shocked and sickened by the irreverence he saw. In the court of the gentiles there was noisy jargon, loud talk and cursing, the bleating of sheep, and the babble of money-changers and vendors of sacrificial animals. Most of all he was outraged by the painted courtesans parading within the temple precincts. Then they went down to the priests’ court to watch the killing of the animals. The bloodstained pavement, the gory hands of the priests, and the sounds of the dying animals were more than this nature-loving boy could stand. He clutched his father’s arm and begged to be taken away. Joseph led him round to see the Gate Beautiful of Corinthian bronze, but Jesus had had enough.

ch05.b019: Joseph and Mary held their peace. Never again did they try to change his mind about the love of God and the mercifulness of the Father in heaven.
ch05.b021: On the day before the Passover Sabbath, flood tides of spiritual illumination swept through the mortal mind of Jesus and filled his heart with affectionate pity for the spiritually blind multitudes assembled for the feast. That night, for the first time in his earth career, there appeared to him an assigned messenger from Salvington, commissioned by Immanuel, who said: “⟦Q 124:6.15⟧The hour has come. It is time that you began to be about your Father’s business.⟦/Q⟧” Even before the heavy responsibilities of the Nazareth family descended upon him, the boy, not quite thirteen, was reminded that the hour had come to begin taking up again the responsibilities of a universe.
ch05.b022: Five Nazareth families kept the Passover with the family of Simon of Bethany, Jesus having persuaded his parents to accept the invitation. They ate the roasted lamb with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, and Jesus, as a new son of the covenant, recounted the origin of the Passover, somewhat disconcerting his parents with remarks reflecting what he had just seen. Already, though he told no one, he was turning over in his mind the propriety of a Passover without the slaughtered lamb, and as the years passed he became determined someday to establish a bloodless Passover. That night he slept little, troubled by revolting dreams of slaughter and suffering. His parents slept little too.
ch05.b023: In the days that followed, young Lazarus showed him Jerusalem, and Jesus discovered the places about the temple where teaching and question conferences were held. As a newly consecrated youth he had to sit outside the rail, and he held back the many questions surging in his mind. On Wednesday he spent the night in Bethany, and from that night Lazarus, Martha, and Mary loved him as if he had been their own brother. He met more than one hundred and fifty young people from many lands and began to desire to travel the world and learn how men everywhere earned their living. Again and again his parents found him sitting alone, head in his hands, profoundly thinking. Sorely perplexed, they longed to have their strangely acting son safely back in Nazareth. Before leaving, they made definite arrangements, with his Nazareth teacher, for his return to an academy at fifteen.
ch05.b024: The Day of Departure · A Night in Jericho
ch05.b025: The Nazareth party gathered near the temple at midforenoon on the first day of the week after the festival. As was the custom, the men traveled in one group and the women in another. Jesus had come up with his mother and the women, but being now a young man of the consecration, he was supposed to return with his father and the men. While the company moved off toward Bethany, Jesus was in the temple, completely absorbed in a discussion of angels, and he did not realize he had been left behind until the conferences adjourned at noon.
ch05.b026: No one missed him. Mary supposed he was with the men; Joseph thought he was with the women, since he had come up with them, leading Mary’s donkey. Only when they reached Jericho and prepared to stop for the night did they discover his absence. They asked the last of the travelers to arrive, and no one had seen him. That night they did not sleep. They went over and over what might have happened to him, recalled his unusual reactions during Passover week, and mildly chided each other for not making sure he was with the group before leaving Jerusalem.
